title: India's exports jump 23% to $44.4 billion in September: what the trade gap means
subtitle: India sold more goods abroad than a year ago, led by electronics and engineering goods, while the trade deficit stood at $30.21 billion.
content_html:
Picture this: in just one month, India sent goods worth about $44.4 billion to other countries. That is phones, machines, fuel, chemicals, jewellery, cereals and more, all packed into ships and planes. The number was 23% higher than in September last year.

The government shared this data on Thursday, 15 October 2026. It also showed that India bought even more from the world than it sold. So what does all this mean, and why should anyone care? Let us break it down.

First, three words to know

Exports are things a country sells to other countries. When a factory in Chennai sends phones to the US, that is an export. Money comes into India.

Imports are things a country buys from other countries. When India buys crude oil from abroad, that is an import. Money goes out of India.

The trade deficit is the gap when imports are bigger than exports. It is how much more a country spent than it earned from selling goods.

The pocket money way to think about it

Imagine a student named Riya. She runs a small lemonade stall on weekends. One month, she earns Rs 44 by selling lemonade to neighbours. That is her "export".

The same month, she spends Rs 75 on lemons, sugar, cups and a new notebook from the shop. That is her "import".

She spent Rs 31 more than she earned. That Rs 31 gap is her "trade deficit". She has to cover it from savings or from other money, like her pocket money.

India in September looked a lot like Riya, only with billions of dollars. It sold $44.40 billion of goods and bought $74.61 billion of goods. The gap was $30.21 billion. And yes, $74.61 billion minus $44.40 billion is exactly $30.21 billion.

Did the gap get smaller or bigger?

Here is the tricky part. Two headlines on the same news site seemed to disagree. One said the deficit narrowed. Another said it widened. Both are right. They just compare September with different months.

  • Compared with last September: the gap got smaller. In September 2025, India exported $36.08 billion and imported $69.08 billion, so the gap was about $33 billion. Now it is $30.21 billion.
  • Compared with August 2026: the gap got bigger. It was $26.86 billion in August, so September's $30.21 billion is higher.

Think of it like a cricket score. A batter may score more than in the same match last year but less than in last week's match. Both facts can be true at once.

Why did the gap shrink over the year? Sales abroad grew faster than purchases. Exports rose 23%, while imports rose only 8%, the slowest import growth in six months.

What did India sell the most?

The rise was spread across many kinds of goods. Here are the big ones:

  • Engineering goods (machines, auto parts, steel items): up 21% to $12.17 billion. That is more than a quarter of all goods exports in the month.
  • Petroleum products (fuels made from crude oil): up 32% to $6.22 billion.
  • Electronic goods (like phones): jumped from $3.11 billion a year ago to $5.31 billion. That is a rise of about 70%, the standout of the month.
  • Gems and jewellery: up 19% to $3.37 billion.
  • Chemicals: up a little over 24% to $2.94 billion.

Smaller items grew fast too. Handicrafts and meat, dairy and poultry products each rose more than 35%. "Other cereals" rose almost 50%.

Not everything went up. Iron ore exports fell 70.8% and cashew fell 39.4%.

Which countries bought the most?

The US stayed India's biggest customer. Exports there rose nearly 48% to $8.03 billion. That is close to one fifth of everything India exported in the month.

Some smaller markets grew even faster. Exports to Singapore rose 169%, to Malaysia about 120% and to Egypt about 90%. Exports to China rose a little over 24% to $1.81 billion.

A few markets slipped. Shipments to the UAE fell 11.8%, to the Netherlands 10.1% and to Saudi Arabia 14.7%.

And what did India buy?

The biggest import was crude oil, the raw oil that becomes petrol and diesel. India spent $18.34 billion on it, up nearly 31%. Electronics imports also jumped nearly 52% to $14.86 billion.

One thing fell sharply: gold. India bought gold worth $1.8 billion, down from $9.61 billion a year ago. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal linked this to a higher customs duty on gold from May. A customs duty is a tax paid when goods enter the country. If the tax on a gold chain goes up, people buy fewer chains from abroad. Less gold buying helped keep the import bill in check.

What about services?

Goods are things you can touch. Services are work you cannot touch, like software, call centres or tourism. India earns a lot here. Services exports in September were estimated at $36.35 billion, almost the same as $36.67 billion a year ago.

Add goods and services together and India's total exports reached about $80.75 billion, up 10.99%. With services counted, the full gap shrank to $13.30 billion, from $14.17 billion a year earlier. Services are like Riya also earning money by tutoring a younger kid. It does not change her lemonade numbers, but it fills a big part of the hole.

The bigger six month picture

From April to September, India's goods exports rose 18.51% to $259.89 billion. Imports rose 16.31% to $437.53 billion. That leaves a goods gap of $177.64 billion for the six months.

September was also the sixth month in a row of double digit export growth, though it was a bit slower than the 26.1% seen in August. Agrawal said goods exports may reach around $500 billion by the end of this financial year, which runs till March 2027.

Why it matters to you

Exports are a growing slice of India's economy. GDP, or gross domestic product, is the total value of everything a country makes in a year, like the full bill of a giant shop. Exports made up 14% of GDP in April to June 2026, up from 11.3% for the year that ended in March 2026.

So the next time someone says "trade deficit", think of Riya's lemonade stall. India is selling more than before, buying a bit more too, and the next monthly numbers will show whether this streak keeps going.
